1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6.name: King's Gambit Accepted: MacLeod Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6.background: Named after Nicholas MacLeod. Joe Gallagher writes that it has never really caught on.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3.name: Vienna Gambit, with Max Lange Defence: Knight Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the second knight and guards e4 instead of hurrying to win the f4 pawn back. The knight on c6 does nothing about Black's problem of holding that pawn, so White can build up the attack while Black's king's side stays unprepared.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 straight away, where only the king defends. Black's knight on c6 does not help to keep the f4 pawn, so White can choose between striking in the centre and attacking the kingside, with the bishop on its best diagonal.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and opens the c1-bishop against the f4 pawn, which the knight on c6 does nothing to defend. It also offers the pawn to the knight: after ...Nxd4 and Nxd4 Black has a check on h4, so White must know what follows.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bc4 g5.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Blachly Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bc4 g5.strategy: Holds the gambit pawn with the g-pawn, the standard way to keep the extra material. The price is a loosened kingside and a pawn on g5 that White can attack at once, so Black has to be ready for sharp play against the king.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bc4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and hits e4, but the pawn simply advances: e5 attacks the knight again and gains time. The knight can go to h5 to guard f4, though it stands on the rim, and f7 stays under the bishop's eye.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bc4 d5.strategy: Returns the gambit pawn for open lines and quick development. Once White takes on d5 the material is level and the game turns on activity, not on the pawn; White's bishop is a strong piece in the middle.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5.strategy: The thematic way to keep the gambit pawn: the g-pawn supports f4 and threatens to kick the f3 knight. Black accepts a loosened kingside and invites a sharp fight, in which White's two developed knights give the attack plenty of fuel.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 Be7.name: Vienna Gambit, with Max Lange Defence: Cunningham Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 Be7.strategy: Develops with the threat of a check on h4 that can cost White the right to castle, since the king would have to step aside. White gains strong central control, and Black counts on the white king's discomfort to compensate.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 d6.strategy: A flexible, solid move: it controls e5 and opens the c8-bishop, leaving the g-pawn to decide later how f4 is held. The pawn is not protected yet, so White's d4, opening the c1-bishop, forces Black to commit the g-pawn anyway.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.B.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 and invites ...g4, with a knight sacrifice to follow, but the attack falls short against the right defence, so White is the one taking the risk. A practical gambit, not a sound plan.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.d.name: Vienna Gambit, with Max Lange Defence: Pierce Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.d.strategy: Challenges the centre at once and opens the c1 bishop against f4. If Black pushes the g-pawn, White usually sacrifices the knight for activity, but the sacrifice leaves White worse against accurate play.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.h.strategy: Hits the g5 pawn at once, but spends a flank pawn while both bishops are still at home. Black keeps the extra pawn and the more comfortable game, and White has to show compensation for it.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.g.strategy: Attacks the f4 pawn with a pawn instead of sacrificing a piece. Black keeps the extra pawn for now, but White gets a level game, with a pawn break against g5 in reserve.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.B.strategy: Chases the knight and keeps the gambit pawn on f4, daring White to play the knight sacrifice. Black accepts a sharp game in which the extra material has to be earned by accurate defence of a king that has not yet castled.

A cautious reply that avoids the knight sacrifice, but it gives away the best of the position: White can build a strong centre while the bishop on c4 keeps f7 under pressure, and Black's extra pawn counts for little.

Opens the c8-bishop and takes e5 under control, keeping ...g4 for later. It is slower than the pawn push: White uses the time to build the centre or to start the attack on f7, and Black must still decide how to meet the sacrifice.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.B.name: Vienna Game: Hamppe-Muzio Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.B.background: Named after the Austrian theoretician Carl Hamppe, it is a close relative of the Muzio Gambit of the King's Gambit.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.B.strategy: Castles and lets the knight go: a piece for a lead in development, a rook on the f-file and a bishop aimed at f7. The attack is real, but Black comes out better with correct defence, and the quiet retreat does better.

Takes the centre and opens the c1-bishop onto f4 before castling, with the knight on f3 offered for the same open lines. White's king stays in the middle a move longer, but the pawn adds a central lead to the attack.
Moves the attacked knight with the idea that works elsewhere, but the black knight stands on c6 and simply takes it. ...Nxe5 wins the piece, and the knight on e5 also attacks the bishop on c4.

Gives up the sacrifice and withdraws the attacked knight, so White stays level on pieces and avoids the attack the other moves invite. White is left a pawn down and ...Qh4+ follows, but it is the safest way out of a bad position.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.B.name: Vienna Gambit, with Max Lange Defence: Hamppe-Muzio Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.B.strategy: Takes the knight, the natural reply. Black is a piece up, but the king is still in the middle, the g-file is open and White's queen and bishop point at the kingside, so Black must hand material back or complete development before the attack lands.

The check looks forcing, but 7.d4 blocks it and attacks the bishop at once, so Black cannot retreat the bishop and take the knight in one move. White gets a strong centre and the initiative against the uncastled king, and Black's winning edge turns into a worse position.

Develops a piece and opens the c8-bishop but turns down the knight: White retreats it with Ne1 and soon wins the f4 pawn back with Rxf4. Black keeps a pawn, yet the winning advantage of 6...gxf3 shrinks to a level game.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.d.strategy: Kicks the knight at once and keeps the f4 pawn. With d4 played, White's c1-bishop already eyes that pawn, so Black asks White to commit the knight or retreat it. Black gains space and time, at the cost of loosening the kingside pawns.

Frees the c8-bishop and covers e5, but lets the moment pass. Without the kick ...g4, White gets time for g3, hitting the f4 pawn, or for a central push, and Black's extra pawn counts for little. Solid, but it hands back the edge.

Develops the bishop against the d4 pawn, but White simply plays d5, driving the knight from c6 with a gain of time. Black stays a pawn up and the position is sound, yet White's centre and development leave the game level.

Aims the bishop at f7 and leaves the knight en prise, ready to give it up for open lines against the king. With a pawn on d4 White also holds a strong centre and has the c1-bishop pointing at f4, which makes the sacrifice more than a bare attack.

Keeps all the pieces by moving the attacked knight to the centre, so White need not sacrifice it. The cost is the king: after ...Qh4+ it has to step aside, since blocking with g3 fails to ...fxg3, and Black keeps the f4 pawn and the initiative.

Wins back the f4 pawn and develops the bishop at once, leaving the knight to be taken. After ...gxf3 White recaptures with the g-pawn and gets an open g-file for the rook, but Black is a piece up for a pawn and the attack is less pointed than the one on f7.

Takes the knight, the most common reply. Black is a piece up, but the king has not castled, the g-file is open and White's queen recaptures with play against the f4 pawn and the bishop eyes f7, so Black has to consolidate quickly.

Develops the bishop against the d4 pawn instead of taking the knight at once. White regains the f4 pawn with Bxf4, and after ...gxf3 Qxf3 the bishop and queen aim at f7, so Black's winning advantage shrinks to a level game.

Guards f7 and the g4 pawn, but the knight sits on the rim and gets in the way of the f8-bishop. White castles or takes back on f4, when the bishop attacks the knight on h6, and Black is cramped and under pressure despite the extra material.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.h.strategy: Kicks the knight, the natural continuation of ...g5, and wins space. The knight's only active square is g5, and the sacrifice that follows brings the attack to the black king, so Black must be ready for a sharp and forcing game.

Takes the pawn, but the king is left without its g-pawn and the g-file opens. White answers with d4, a strong centre and quick development, and Black's extra pawns on f4 and h4 cannot both be held, so the capture gives back more than it gains.

Develops the bishop and protects the rook on h8 but leaves g5 to be taken: after hxg5 the extra pawn is gone, and taking back with the queen loses the queen to the knight on f3. White gets the h-file and a free hand in development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.h.name: Vienna Gambit, with Max Lange Defence: Hamppe-Allgaier Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.h.strategy: The knight jumps into the black camp, protected by the h4 pawn and eyeing f7, but once ...h6 attacks it no square is safe and it has to be sacrificed on f7. White gets an exposed king for the piece, though modern theory finds the attack unsound.

Takes the attacked knight home instead of sacrificing it, and keeps the h4 pawn guarded: ...Qxh4+ runs into the rook. White is a pawn down and has lost time, with Black's f4 and g4 pawns cramping the kingside, so he must prove his compensation through development and a central break.
Attacks the g4 pawn but blocks the rook's defence of h4: ...Qxh4+ wins that pawn with check and forces the king to move or the g-pawn to block. White has retreated and still lost a second pawn.
Hangs the knight: the knight on c6 simply takes it, and the pawn push that follows only chases Black's piece away. White has given up a whole piece for nothing.
Attacks the knight, which has no safe retreat and must sacrifice itself on f7. Black forces matters and wins a piece for a pawn, then has to survive the attack on a king pulled into the open.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.h.name: Vienna Gambit, with Max Lange Defence: Hamppe-Allgaier Gambit, Alapin Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5 5.h.strategy: Supports the g4 pawn with the c8 bishop and covers e5, but leaves the knight on g5 where it is, still pressing on f7. A slower reply than driving the knight away, so Black has to be ready for the sacrifice on f7 anyway.

Covers f7 and the g4 pawn with a piece instead of driving the knight away, but it is a rim knight in front of the f8-bishop, and the knight on g5 is left where it is. White builds a full centre and wins back the f4 pawn, and Black ends up defending.
